items.en: The Merit of the Four Immeasurable Minds

zh: 第五、釋四無量功德，即為二：一者、現世；二者、未來世。一、現世功德者，如佛《阿含》中說：「若入慈心三昧者，現世得五種功德：一、入火不燒；二、中毒不死；三、兵刃不傷；四、終不橫死；五、善神擁護。」以利益無量眾生故，得無量福德。二、未來功德者，善修四無量心，若生色界，多作梵王，以無量心廣攝眾生故；若於初禪得，即作初禪王，乃至四禪亦爾。
en: Fifth, explaining the merit of the four immeasurable minds: this itself has two parts — merit in this present life; and merit in the life to come.

First, as for merit in this present life: as the Buddha says in the Āgamas: "One who enters the samādhi of loving-kindness attains five kinds of merit in this present life: entering fire, one is not burned; encountering poison, one does not die; struck by weapons, one is not wounded; one never dies an untimely death; and one is protected and guarded by wholesome spirits." Because of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, one attains immeasurable merit in turn.

Second, as for merit in the life to come: one who cultivates the four immeasurable minds well, should they be born into the form realm, for the most part becomes a Brahmā king, since the immeasurable minds embrace sentient beings so broadly. Should this attainment be reached within the first dhyāna, one becomes king of the first dhyāna's heaven, and the same holds, further still, all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well.

zh: 問曰：三藏中但說初禪號娑婆世界主、梵天王，今何故說乃至四禪悉有梵王？答曰：《纓絡經》中明四禪，禪禪並有梵王。問曰：若爾，佛何以故說慈報生梵天上？答曰：以梵天眾生所尊，皆聞皆識故。佛在天竺國常多婆羅門，婆羅門法所有福德盡願生梵天，若聞行慈生梵天，聞多信教，修行慈法，以是故說行慈生梵天上。復次，斷婬欲天皆名為梵，說梵則攝四禪、四無色定，如五戒中律儀，但說一種不妄語則攝三事。復次，若於四禪中修四無量心，隨是禪中，悉得受生。既隨禪生無量心，福德大故，果報亦應有異，豈得生於彼天而無君民之別？復次，如佛於《仁王經》說十八梵，亦應有王民之異。又云四禪中有大靜王，而佛於三藏中但說初禪有大梵王者，以初禪內有覺觀心。雖則有語言法主領下地眾生為便，上地無此，故不別出。
en: Question: the Tripiṭaka speaks only of the first dhyāna's own heaven as bearing the title Lord of the Sahā World, the Brahmā King — why, then, is it now said that Brahmā kings are present all the way through the fourth dhyāna as well? Answer: the Yingluo Sūtra, in clarifying the four dhyānas, states that a Brahmā king is present within each and every one of the four dhyānas' own heavens.

Question: if this is so, why does the Buddha say that the karmic reward of loving-kindness is birth in the Brahmā heaven specifically? Answer: because the Brahmā heaven is honored by sentient beings, heard of by all, and known by all. The Buddha, while in the land of India, was constantly surrounded by many brāhmaṇas, and the brāhmaṇa teaching holds that every merit whatsoever should ultimately aim at rebirth in the Brahmā heaven; hence, hearing that practicing loving-kindness leads to birth in the Brahmā heaven, many among them, upon hearing this, came to believe and follow the teaching, cultivating and practicing the dharma of loving-kindness — hence it is said, for this very reason, that practicing loving-kindness leads to birth in the Brahmā heaven.

Furthermore: every heaven that has severed lustful desire is named, in general, "Brahmā" — and so speaking of "Brahmā" already encompasses the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations together, just as, among the five precepts' own moral codes, speaking of the single precept against false speech alone is already understood to encompass three matters as well. Furthermore: if the four immeasurable minds are cultivated within any of the four dhyānas, one is bound to be reborn according to that very dhyāna. Since one is thus reborn according to whichever dhyāna the immeasurable minds were cultivated within, and the merit involved is itself great, the karmic result, too, should correspondingly differ — how, then, could one possibly be reborn into that heaven with no distinction at all between ruler and ruled? Furthermore, as the Buddha says in the Humane Kings Sūtra, there are eighteen Brahmā heavens, and these, too, should have their own distinction between ruler and ruled. It is also said that there is a Great Tranquil King present within the fourth dhyāna as well; and, as for why the Buddha, within the Tripiṭaka, speaks only of the first dhyāna as having a Great Brahmā King, this is because the first dhyāna alone still has initial thought and sustained reflection present within it — and so, since it still has the dharma of language, it is convenient for it to serve as the ruling lord over the beings of the stages below; the higher stages have no such need for this, and so are not separately named.

zh: 問曰：若爾，佛何故說四無量功德，慈心好修善修，福德極遍淨天；悲心好修善修，福德極虛空處；喜心好修善修，福德極識處；捨心好修善修，福德極無所有處？云何言慈果報應生梵天上？答曰：佛法不可思議，隨眾生應度者如是說。復次，從慈定起，入三禪易；從悲定起，向虛空處易；從喜定起，入識處易；捨定起，入無所有處易。復次，慈心願令眾生得樂，此果報自應受樂。三界中，遍淨天最為樂故，言福德極遍淨。悲心觀眾生老病殘害，行者憐愍心生，云何令得離苦？若除內苦，外苦復來；若為除外苦，心苦復來。行者思惟：「有身則有苦，唯有無身，乃得無苦。」虛空能破色，是故福德極虛空處。喜心欲與眾生樂，心識樂者，心得離身，如鳥出籠。虛空處，心雖得出身，猶繫心虛空處無得礙。於一切法中皆有心識，識得自在無邊故，以喜福極在識處。捨心者，捨眾生中苦樂，故得真法，所謂無所有處，以是故，捨心福極無所有處。
en: Question: if this is so, why does the Buddha then speak of the four immeasurable minds' merit in this other way — that loving-kindness, cultivated well, has its merit reaching its utmost in the Heaven of Universal Purity; compassion, cultivated well, has its merit reaching its utmost in the sphere of boundless space; sympathetic joy, cultivated well, has its merit reaching its utmost in the sphere of boundless consciousness; and equanimity, cultivated well, has its merit reaching its utmost in the sphere of nothingness — how, then, can it also be said that loving-kindness's own karmic result leads to birth in the Brahmā heaven? Answer: the Buddhadharma is inconceivable, spoken of in whatever way suits whichever sentient beings are to be delivered by it at the time. Furthermore: arising from the concentration of loving-kindness, one enters the third dhyāna easily; arising from the concentration of compassion, one turns toward the sphere of boundless space easily; arising from the concentration of sympathetic joy, one enters the sphere of boundless consciousness easily; and arising from the concentration of equanimity, one enters the sphere of nothingness easily.

Furthermore: the mind of loving-kindness vows that sentient beings attain happiness, and so its own karmic result naturally receives happiness in turn — and, among the three realms, the Heaven of Universal Purity is the very happiest of all, hence its merit is said to reach its utmost there. The mind of compassion contemplates sentient beings growing old, falling ill, and being harmed, a mind of pity arising in the practitioner — how, then, might they be freed from suffering? If the inward suffering is removed, outward suffering returns; and if the outward suffering is removed instead, mental suffering returns in its place. The practitioner reflects: "Wherever there is a body, there is suffering; only where there is no body at all can there be freedom from suffering." Since empty space is able to break through form entirely, its merit is said to reach its utmost in the sphere of boundless space. The mind of sympathetic joy wishes to give sentient beings happiness — and one whose mind and consciousness attain happiness gains a mind freed from the body, like a bird escaping its cage; in the sphere of boundless space, although the mind has already escaped the body, it remains bound to the sphere of space itself, still unable to move freely — whereas, within every dharma whatsoever, mind and consciousness are already present, and consciousness itself is boundless and free; hence sympathetic joy's merit reaches its utmost in the sphere of boundless consciousness. The mind of equanimity relinquishes both suffering and happiness among sentient beings, and so attains the true dharma of what is called the sphere of nothingness; hence equanimity's own merit reaches its utmost in the sphere of nothingness.

zh: 若作如是明四無量心功德，但諸聖人智慧方便自在故如是，非諸凡夫。何以故？凡夫之人住初禪乃至四禪，修四無量，隨禪受報，不能方便巧入無色修四無量。復次，佛知未來世諸弟子鈍根故，分別著諸法，錯說四無量相，是四無量心，聖人所知，眾生緣故，但是有漏，但緣欲界故，無色界中無。所以者何？無色界不緣欲界故。為斷如是人妄見故，說四無量心。無色界中亦以四無量心普緣十方眾生故，不重言不緣無色界。如是說者，多存法緣、無緣。復次，行者若於眾生緣中具足入法緣、無緣，是時眾生緣四無量心是摩訶衍。復次，菩薩發菩提心，行菩薩道，此眾生緣四無量心，雖是凡夫所行，亦應知應證。證已，以不可得空無所著，善巧方便，即能於此定中具足一切善法，度諸眾生，即是行菩薩道。復次，四無量心中觀行功德眾多，更欲論餘事，不具明也。
en: If the merit of the four immeasurable minds is explained in this way, this holds only because the noble ones' own wisdom and skillful means are themselves free and unobstructed — it does not hold for ordinary people. Why is this? Ordinary people, abiding within the first dhyāna all the way through the fourth, cultivate the four immeasurable minds and receive their karmic result according to whichever dhyāna they cultivated them in, unable to skillfully enter the formless realm and cultivate the four immeasurable minds there as well.

Furthermore: the Buddha, knowing that future disciples would be of dull faculty, clinging to distinctions among dharmas, and so might mistakenly describe the mark of the four immeasurable minds — these four immeasurable minds, as known by the noble ones, take sentient beings as their object, and so are contaminated; and, since they take only the desire realm as their object, they are absent within the formless realm. Why is this? Because the formless realm does not take the desire realm as its object at all. In order to sever such a mistaken view as this, the four immeasurable minds are spoken of as they are here; within the formless realm, too, the four immeasurable minds broadly take the ten directions' sentient beings as their object, and so it is not said again separately that they fail to take the formless realm as their object. Those who speak in this way, for the most part, are describing the immeasurable minds that take dharma as their object, and those that are objectless.

Furthermore: should the practitioner, within the immeasurable minds that take sentient beings as their object, fully enter also those that take dharma as their object and those that are objectless, then, at this point, the four immeasurable minds that take sentient beings as their object are themselves the Mahāyāna. Furthermore: the bodhisattva, having given rise to the bodhi-mind and practicing the bodhisattva path, should know and realize this very immeasurable mind that takes sentient beings as its object as well, even though it is, in itself, a practice of the ordinary person. Having realized it, through the unfindable emptiness of non-attachment, and skillful means, one is thereby able to be complete in every wholesome dharma within this very concentration, liberating all sentient beings — this is precisely the practice of the bodhisattva path. Furthermore: the contemplative merit within the four immeasurable minds is itself manifold; wishing to discuss the remaining matters further would exceed what can be given here in full.

The apparent contradiction resolved here — loving-kindness leading to the Brahmā heaven in one teaching, but to the Heaven of Universal Purity's own third-dhyāna bliss in another — gets the treatise's characteristic non-resolution: both are true, spoken to different audiences ("the brāhmaṇas of India already revered the Brahmā heaven, so that framing met them where they were") rather than one superseding the other. The closing move echoes the one that closed fascicle 5, with a careful qualification: the treatise calls it a mistaken account by future disciples of dull faculty to declare flatly that the four immeasurable minds are contaminated and absent from the formless realm. What is an ordinary person's practice is specifically the immeasurable mind that takes sentient beings as its object — and yet a bodhisattva must still know and realize it, because it is precisely the ground on which the immeasurable minds that take dharma as their object, and those that are objectless, are eventually built. This closes the four immeasurable minds — mundane dhyāna's second of three sections — in full.

items.en: A Deviant Path: The Concentration of No-Thought

zh: 次四無量心後，應釋無想定。何以故？有諸外道深厭有為心識生滅，欲求涅槃寂靜常樂，既無智慧，不知真實，得四禪時，不見細色之過，但覺心識生滅虛誑，則厭患其心。既不知破色斷色繫縛，直以邪智滅却其心，邪法相應，心無憶想，謂證涅槃。既未斷色繫縛，若捨命時，即生無想天中，猶是色界生死，不得解脫，亦名客天。猶如阿那含人修五品熏禪，為色界思惟惑未盡，寄生色界，亦名客天。此無想定既是邪法，非佛弟子所修，今欲具足明三界定，所以略明，示知邪正相耳。
en: Next, following the four immeasurable minds, the concentration of no-thought should be explained. Why is this? There are non-Buddhist practitioners who grow deeply weary of the arising and ceasing of conditioned mind and consciousness, wishing to seek nirvāṇa as a still, permanent happiness; yet, lacking true wisdom, and not knowing the truth of the matter, upon attaining the fourth dhyāna, they fail to perceive the fault present within its own subtle form, and are aware only of mind and consciousness's own arising and ceasing as illusory and false, growing weary of and troubled by this very mind. Not knowing how to break through form and sever the bondage of form, they simply use a deviant wisdom to extinguish the mind directly instead — corresponding with this deviant dharma, the mind free of any thought at all, they take this to be the realization of nirvāṇa.

Since the bondage of form has not, in fact, been severed at all, when their life ends, they are reborn into the heaven of no-thought instead — still nothing more than birth-and-death within the form realm, never actually attaining liberation — also called a "guest heaven." This is comparable to the anāgāmin who cultivates the five-grade dhyāna of habituation: since the form realm's own delusions to be severed on the path of cultivation have not yet been entirely exhausted, they, too, take temporary lodging within the form realm, likewise called a "guest heaven." Since this concentration of no-thought is itself a deviant dharma, and not something a disciple of the Buddha would ever cultivate, it is given here only in brief, for the sake of completeness in clarifying the concentrations of the three realms, simply to show and make known the marks of the deviant and the correct.

This deviant path completes the diagnostic sketch this fascicle opened with — the non-Buddhist practitioner who "sees a defect in the very presence of mind and consciousness" and tries to extinguish the mind directly rather than understanding it. The distinction being drawn is precise: mistaking the mere absence of thought for liberation, without ever actually breaking through form's own bondage, produces only another form of rebirth (a "guest heaven," temporary lodging rather than a true home) — a warning that a still, thoughtless mind is not automatically the same thing as realization, however peaceful it may feel from within.

quiz.q: According to the Āgamas, one who enters the samādhi of loving-kindness gains five merits in this life. Which is NOT among them?
quiz.why: The five are not burned by fire, not killed by poison, not wounded by weapons, no untimely death, and protection by wholesome spirits. The heavenly eye is not listed.

quiz.q: What is the merit in the life to come for one who cultivates the immeasurable minds well?
options: born in the form realm, one mostly becomes a Brahmā king; attained in the first dhyāna, king of that heaven, and so up to the fourth
quiz.why: Born in the form realm, one mostly becomes a Brahmā king, because the immeasurable minds embrace beings broadly; the king of whichever dhyāna heaven one attained.

quiz.q: The Tripiṭaka names a Brahmā king only for the first dhyāna. On what scripture does the text say all four have one?
options: the Yingluo Sūtra: a Brahmā king in each of the four dhyānas
quiz.why: The Yingluo Sūtra states that each of the four dhyāna heavens has a Brahmā king. The Humane Kings Sūtra's eighteen Brahmā heavens is a further support given later.

quiz.q: Why does "Brahmā" encompass the four dhyānas and the formless concentrations, and what comparison is given?
options: the formless realms are in the first dhyāna
the Brahmā King rules the three realms
every heaven that has severed lust is called Brahmā, as the single precept against false speech encompasses three matters
Brahmā is another name for the Buddha
quiz.why: Every heaven free of lust is called Brahmā, so the name covers the four dhyānas and formless concentrations, as mentioning false speech alone covers three matters among the precepts.

quiz.q: Why does the Buddha, in the Tripiṭaka, speak of a Great Brahmā King only for the first dhyāna?
options: the Great Brahmā practices only loving-kindness
the first dhyāna has initial thought and reflection, hence language, convenient for ruling the realms below; higher stages lack this
quiz.why: Only the first dhyāna has initial thought and sustained reflection, and so language, which is convenient for ruling the realms below; higher stages have no such need.

quiz.q: When each immeasurable mind is cultivated well, where does its merit reach its utmost?
options: all in neither perception nor non-perception
loving-kindness: Universal Purity; compassion: boundless space; joy: boundless consciousness; equanimity: nothingness
quiz.why: Loving-kindness reaches its utmost in the Heaven of Universal Purity, compassion in boundless space, sympathetic joy in boundless consciousness, equanimity in nothingness.

quiz.q: Why does compassion's merit reach its utmost in the sphere of boundless space?
options: removing one suffering brings another; where there is a body there is suffering, and space breaks through form
quiz.why: Wherever there is a body there is suffering; only without a body is one free of it, and space breaks through form. The happiest heaven, Universal Purity, belongs to loving-kindness.

quiz.q: To whom does this account of the merit reaching the formless spheres apply?
options: only to the noble ones; ordinary people receive results according to the dhyāna and cannot enter the formless realm to cultivate them
quiz.why: It holds only for the noble ones, whose wisdom and skillful means are free; ordinary people receive results according to their dhyāna.

quiz.q: How does the text describe why non-Buddhists enter the concentration of no-thought?
options: having realized the eight noble lineages
not perceiving the fault of subtle form, they grow weary of mind's arising and ceasing and extinguish the mind with deviant wisdom
quiz.why: They fail to see the fault of subtle form, grow weary only of mind's arising and ceasing, and, not knowing how to break through form, extinguish the mind with deviant wisdom, calling it nirvāṇa.

quiz.q: Why is the heaven of no-thought also called a "guest heaven," and with whom is it compared?
options: form's bondage is not severed; like the anāgāmin cultivating the five-grade dhyāna, it is a temporary lodging in the form realm
quiz.why: With form's bondage unsevered, one is reborn in the heaven of no-thought, still within the form realm's birth and death; like the anāgāmin with remaining delusion, it is a guest lodging.
